title: Can additive squares be avoided over the integers?
credit: T. C. Brown and A. R. Freedman (1987); G. Pirillo and S. Varricchio (1994); see also Halbeisen-Hungerbühler, Cassaigne-Currie-Schaeffer-Shallit.
premise_risks: Zhang 2026 preprint (arXiv:2610.02215) is unrefereed but only cited as context
The problem is sometimes informally attributed to its askers, but it is not a person-named conjecture
plain: An additive square in a sequence of integers is a block of 2k consecutive terms whose first half and second half have the same sum (for example 1 3 | 2 2). Is there a finite set of integers S and an infinite sequence with all terms in S that contains no additive square? Such sequences exist over a finite subset of the plane lattice Z², and over Z one can avoid additive cubes (three adjacent blocks of equal length and equal sum), but no one knows whether squares can be avoided over Z.
math: Decide whether there exist a finite set $S\subset\mathbb{Z}$ and $w:\mathbb{N}\to S$ such that for all $i\ge0$ and $k\ge1$, $\sum_{j=i}^{i+k-1}w(j)\neq\sum_{j=i+k}^{i+2k-1}w(j)$. Equivalently, by compactness: is there a finite $S\subset\mathbb Z$ for which arbitrarily long finite words over $S$ avoid additive squares?
